content.text: Computing innovations are built by people — and people carry biases, conscious and unconscious, into everything they create. When those biases get encoded into algorithms or embedded in the data used to train and run computing innovations, the result is computing bias. Computing bias is not just a technical problem — it is a social and ethical problem because biased computing innovations can cause real harm to real people at massive scale.

content.definition: Computing innovations can reflect existing human biases through biases written into algorithms or biases in the data used. Biases can be embedded at all levels of software development. Programmers should take action to reduce bias.

content.text: The CED identifies two distinct sources of computing bias: biases written INTO THE ALGORITHMS themselves, and biases IN THE DATA used by the innovation. Both are important and produce different kinds of problems. An algorithm can be biased even with unbiased data, and biased data can produce biased outputs even from an algorithm designed without bias. In practice, both sources often exist simultaneously.
Where Does Computing Bias Come From?

content.term: Where does computing bias come from?
content.definition: Computing bias can come from biases written directly into the algorithms, or from biases present in the data used to train or run the innovation. Biases can be embedded at all levels of software development — not just in the final product.

rows: Bias in the algorithm
The rules, weights, or logic of the algorithm itself encode biased assumptions about the world
A loan approval algorithm gives less weight to income earned from certain types of jobs that are more common in minority communities — not because of the data, but because of how it was programmed
Bias in the data
The training or input data does not represent all groups equally — the algorithm learns from skewed data and produces skewed results
A facial recognition system trained mostly on light-skinned faces performs poorly on darker-skinned faces — the bias came from the data, not the algorithm logic
Both simultaneously
Biased data AND biased algorithm design compound each other
A hiring algorithm trained on historical data from a company that rarely hired women, plus algorithmic rules that penalize career gaps (common for caregivers), doubly disadvantages women

content.text: Biases Can Be Embedded at ALL Levels

content.term: How should programmers address computing bias?
content.definition: Programmers should take action to reduce bias in algorithms used for computing innovations as a way of combating existing human biases. This requires vigilance at all levels of development since biases can be embedded anywhere in the process.

content.text: Biases can be embedded at all levels of software development — not just at the final testing stage. This is a crucial point: bias is not something that only appears at the end of development that you can find and fix before release. It can enter at every stage of the development process.

rows: Requirements gathering
Who is consulted about what the system should do — and whose needs are ignored
A voice recognition system designed and tested by a team of native English speakers never considers non-native speakers or regional accents
Data collection
What data is collected, from whom, and what is excluded
A medical diagnosis algorithm trained only on data from wealthy urban hospitals — underrepresents rural, low-income, and minority patients
Algorithm design
What rules, weights, and optimization targets are chosen
A recidivism prediction algorithm that uses ZIP code as a factor — ZIP code correlates with race due to historical housing discrimination
Testing and evaluation
Who tests the system and what inputs are used
A facial recognition system tested only on faces of the developers' demographic — bias in darker-skinned faces is never detected
Deployment
Where and how the system is deployed and who reviews its decisions
An automated hiring tool deployed without human review — biased decisions go undetected and unchallenged

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Bias does not just enter computing innovations at one stage — it can enter at EVERY stage of development. This is why reducing bias requires attention throughout the entire development process, not just a final bias check before release.
Computing bias is not a theoretical concern — it has caused real harm in high-stakes situations. Understanding concrete examples helps identify bias when you encounter it on the AP exam.

rows: Facial recognition systems
Data bias — trained mostly on light-skinned faces
Higher error rates for darker-skinned individuals — wrong identifications in law enforcement use have led to false arrests
Hiring algorithms
Data bias — trained on historical hiring data reflecting past discrimination
Perpetuates and automates historical discrimination — penalizes applicants from underrepresented groups
Recidivism prediction tools (used in criminal sentencing)
Algorithm and data bias — ZIP code, poverty factors correlate with race
Black defendants rated as higher risk at higher rates — affects sentencing and parole decisions
Natural language processing systems
Data bias — trained on internet text reflecting societal biases
Associates certain names or words with negative qualities based on cultural biases in the training data
Medical diagnosis algorithms
Data bias — trained primarily on data from certain demographic groups
Less accurate for patients who are underrepresented in training data — can miss diagnoses or suggest wrong treatments

content.text: Why Computing Bias Matters at Scale

Human bias in individual decisions has always existed. What makes computing bias different and especially concerning is scale. A biased human loan officer might make biased decisions for a few hundred applicants per year. A biased algorithm can make biased decisions for millions of applicants instantly. Computing amplifies bias in the same way it amplifies everything else — making the effects far larger and more difficult to challenge or appeal.

rows: Affects one person or a small number at a time
Can affect millions of people simultaneously
Decision-maker can be questioned and held accountable
Algorithm's reasoning is often opaque — difficult to understand or challenge
Decisions can be reviewed case by case
Scale makes individual review impractical without specifically designed auditing systems
Bias can be reduced through training and oversight of individual humans
Bias must be addressed at the design and data level — harder to fix after deployment
Each decision is made fresh with human judgment
Once biased, the algorithm applies the same bias consistently to every case — no natural variation

content.text: Programmer Responsibility: Taking Action to Reduce Bias

Programmers should take action to reduce bias in algorithms used for computing innovations as a way of combating existing human biases. This is not just a technical responsibility — it is an ethical one. Bias in computing innovations reflects and amplifies human biases in society. Programmers who build these systems have a responsibility to actively work against that amplification.

items: Audit training data for representation — ensure data includes diverse groups proportionally and identify underrepresented populations
Test systems on diverse inputs — evaluate performance separately for different demographic groups to identify performance gaps
Include diverse perspectives in development teams — people from different backgrounds are more likely to identify biases that affect their own communities
Build in human review for high-stakes decisions — automated systems making decisions about hiring, lending, or criminal justice need human oversight
Document known limitations — be transparent about what groups the system has been tested on and where its limitations lie
Monitor systems after deployment — bias can emerge or worsen over time as the world changes while the system stays static

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The AP exam tests three specific things about computing bias: (1) Computing innovations can REFLECT existing human biases through biases in algorithms or data. (2) Biases can be embedded at ALL LEVELS of software development — not just in data. (3) Programmers SHOULD TAKE ACTION to reduce bias. When asked what a responsible programmer should do about computing bias, the answer is: take action to reduce it — not just acknowledge it exists.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students sometimes think computing bias only comes from 'bad' or intentionally discriminatory programmers. This is wrong — bias can be unintentional, embedded in data that seems neutral, or a consequence of systemic inequalities in the world. A programmer who genuinely tries to be fair can still produce a biased system if they do not actively look for and address bias in their data and algorithms.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: Computing innovations can reflect existing human biases through biases written INTO THE ALGORITHMS or biases IN THE DATA used
Biases can be embedded at ALL LEVELS of software development — requirements, data collection, algorithm design, testing, and deployment
Computing bias is not always intentional — it can result from unrepresentative data or biased design choices made without awareness
Programmers SHOULD TAKE ACTION to reduce bias in algorithms as a way of combating existing human biases
Computing bias can cause real harm at massive scale — especially in high-stakes systems like hiring, lending, and criminal justice
Reducing bias requires attention throughout the entire development process — not just a final check before release
Actions to reduce bias include: auditing training data for representation, testing on diverse inputs, including diverse development teams, and building in human review for high-stakes decisions
